name: Gadsup
catalog_citation: Frantz, Chester I. & Marjorie E. Frantz. 1966. Gadsup phoneme and toneme units. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 5 (Pacific Linguistics A-7), 1-12. Canberra: ANU. DOI:10.15144/PL-A7.1 (sealang.net open PDF).
catalog_quote: 2. SUPRASEGMENTAL PHONEMES. Four contrastive tones have been noted in Gadsup: high, low, up-glide, and down-glide. We shall first indicate the various contrasts, and then proceed to amplify why it appears advisable to analyze the glides as units and not as sequences of two level tonemes. ... 2.4. Stress. Stress is nonphonemic. In analogous environments syllables: (1) with a, e, or o have more stress than those with ʌ, i, or u; (2) with high, rising, or falling tones have more stress than those with low; (3) with a phonetic stop onset have more stress than those with nonstop onset. Combinations of these features lead to varying degrees of non-contrastive stress.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Frantz & Frantz 1966 PDF (section 2 on p.5; section 2.4 'Stress is nonphonemic...' on printed p.9, the record says p.10 — a one-page locator slip worth correcting but not a quote problem). The source is the primary and only phonological description of Gadsup that addresses stress; there is no reference grammar. Every later description I could open — SIL OPD (Frantz-checked 1995), Cahill 2011 (own consultant data), Pennington 2014 (pitch tracks, word-melody reanalysis with 7 melodies and occasional lexical accents), DYL 2016 — treats Gadsup as a lexical tone language and gives no positional stress rule, so the 'tonal, no stress rule' coding stands. Pennington 2014 could be added to the record as a corroborating/refining source (word-tone rather than syllable-tone analysis; 'lexical accents' are tonal-association accents, not stress). WALS 13

sources.citation: Pennington, Ryan. 2014. Tone in Gadsup noun phrases [slides 'Gadsup tone', 35 pp]. Paper presented at LSPNG 2014, Divine Word University, Madang; SIL-PNG / REAP archive.
sources.quote: Instrumental (pitch-track) reanalysis of Aseranka-dialect Gadsup from one speaker: 'Previous analysis Frantz & Frantz 1973, Cahill 2011: 4 tonemes H, L, F, R'; proposes a word-tone system: 'Gadsup has 7 bona fide tonal melodies ... L, H, LH, HL, LHL, HLH, LHLH', 'The TBU is the (vocalic) mora', 'Some words have lexical accents which pull the tonal melody inward'. No statement about stress.

sources.quote: 'Gadsup (Trans-New Guinea; Frantz and Frantz 1973) exhibits a completely different system. A syllable may exhibit High, Low, Rising, or Falling tones, with tonal contrasts available on every syllable ... the TBU is the syllable'. Own consultant data on tone perturbation; nothing on stress.
